title: Endocranial development in non-avian dinosaurs reveals an ontogenetic brain trajectory distinct from extant archosaurs

paper_content.abstract: Modern birds possess highly encephalized brains that evolved from non-avian dinosaurs. Evolutionary shifts in developmental timing, namely juvenilization of adult phenotypes, have been proposed as a driver of head evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition, including brain morphology. Testing this hypothesis requires a sufficient developmental sampling of brain morphology in non-avian dinosaurs. In this study, we harness brain endocasts of a postnatal growth series of the ornithischian dinosaur Psittacosaurus and several other immature and mature non-avian dinosaurs to investigate how evolutionary changes to brain development are implicated in the origin of the avian brain. Using three-dimensional characterization of neuroanatomical shape across archosaurian reptiles, we demonstrate that (i) the brain of non-avian dinosaurs underwent a distinct developmental trajectory compared to alligators and crown birds; (ii) ornithischian and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs shared a similar developmental trajectory, suggesting that their derived trajectory evolved in their common ancestor; and (iii) the evolutionary shift in developmental trajectories is partly consistent with paedomorphosis underlying overall brain shape evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition; however, the heterochronic signal is not uniform across time and neuroanatomical region suggesting a highly mosaic acquisition of the avian brain form.
paper_content.introduction:
The evolutionary origin of highly encephalized brains in modern birds is not only of interest to avian neuroscience but also has implications for how large brains evolve across vertebrates, including humans. Disentangling how the brain of crown birds (“Aves”) evolved requires study of brain anatomy ancestral to crown birds—that of non-avian dinosaurs. Using skulls and cephalic endocasts (internal molds of the braincase) as proxies for brain shape and size, previous studies have revealed that the evolutionary assembly of the avian brain form proceeded in a mosaic and homoplastic manner from the ancestral dinosaurian pattern1–11. While the tempo and mode of avian brain evolution is well established by recent studies, the mechanism underlying major neuroanatomical transformation along the dinosaur-bird transition remains uncertain3,12. Previous studies have proposed that a mixture of heterochronic processes within the cranium, particularly progenesis (truncation of the ancestral developmental period) and accelerated peramorphosis (evolutionarily driven increases in developmental rates), may underlie major changes to the brain architecture from ancestral archosaurian forms to crown birds3,11–16. However, a good developmental series of neuroanatomical morphologies for non-avian dinosaurs has been lacking to date; and crucial evidence is needed for a reliable inference of evolutionary shifts in brain development along the dinosaur-bird transition.

In this study, we examine an ontogenetic series of endocasts of the ornithischian dinosaur Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis, spanning perinatal to somatically mature individuals (<1-, 7-, 8-, and 10-year-old individuals) that were recently described17,18 (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Fig. 1). This allows for an unprecedented look into how the neuroanatomy of a non-avialan dinosaur species changes with age. We incorporate this developmental dataset into an interspecific dataset of archosaurian endocranial morphology which also includes postnatal ontogenetic series of the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) and American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) as an outgroup3 (Fig. 1a, b). Moreover, we include immature specimens of additional non-avialan dinosaurs17–21 (Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, tyrannosaurids, Zanabazar, and an unnamed troodontid; Supplementary Data 1) to further define the overall developmental axis of brain morphology in non-avialan dinosaurs (i.e., excluding Archaeopteryx considered here to be a basal avialan). Using a landmark-based geometric morphometric characterization of endocranial shape (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Table 1), the study aims to investigate how the magnitude and direction of developmental shape changes in brain morphology in non-avian dinosaurs compare to (i) the domestic chicken and the American alligator and (ii) the principal axis of brain shape evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition to evaluate whether heterochronic processes, particularly progenesis, underlie the origins of the highly derived avian brain. In our reporting, endocranial regions are referred to by their underlying soft-tissue features (i.e., “cerebrum” rather than “impression of the cerebrum”).

Here, we show that the endocranial form of non-avian dinosaurs developed and evolved uniquely when compared to crown birds and Alligator mississippiensis. We demonstrate that ornithischians and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs share a common shape-to-size relationship that guides their brain development and evolution. Regional morphometric analyses of endocranial developmental trajectories reveal that non-avian dinosaurs collectively exhibit a mosaic of avian and crocodilian modes of allometric trajectories wherein the cerebrum and optic lobe regions of immature non-avialan dinosaurs resemble those of extant birds whereas the brainstem region follows the trajectory of the crocodilians. Our results thus support a paedomorphic trend occurring along the dinosaur-bird transition that is localized to some but not all regions of the brain.
paper_content.results:
Endocranial shape morphospaces
To visualize total and regional endocranial shape variation, morphospaces were constructed based on principal components (PC) axes of endocast shape data (Fig. 2). In the morphospace of total endocranial shape, lower PC1 scores are associated with posterolaterally expanded cerebra, ventrally oriented optic lobes, anteroposteriorly compact hindbrains, and higher dorsoventral flexion with respect to both cephalic and pontine flexures as defined by Lautenschlager and Hübner22. Lower PC2 scores correspond to elongated cerebra, dorsoventrally extended optic lobes, anteroposteriorly shortened cerebellum, and greater dorsoventral flexion along the brainstem. As expected, total endocast shape data closely reflect the results found in previous geometric morphometric work where crown birds, alligators, and non-avian dinosaurs individually form clusters along PC1, with Archaeopteryx positioned between crown birds and non-avialan archosaurs along PC1 (Fig. 2a)3. Ornithischian and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs overlap with each other, and mature individuals of both groups strongly overlap with mature endocranial shape of Alligator along PC1 and PC2. With the exception of 7-year-old Psittacosaurus (IVPP V12731), endocasts of immature non-avialan dinosaurs generally exhibit lower PC1 scores closer to the crown bird cluster. The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid (IGM 100/1126), as well as the small-bodied, purportedly immature tyrannosaurid specimen (CMNH 7541), occupy an intermediary position between crown birds and non-avialan archosaurs along PC1 (Fig. 2a). All other juvenile taxa maintain similar PC2 scores as CMNH 7541 but have higher PC1 scores. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid (IGM 100/1126), overlap in PC2 values as neo- and perinatal Gallus (Fig. 2a).

During development, the immature non-avialan dinosaur endocasts exhibit a posterolaterally expanded cerebrum, more ventrally oriented optic lobes, anteroposteriorly compressed hindbrain, and greater degree of dorsoventral flexion. In the case of IVPP V15451 and IGM 100/1126 (perinate Psittacosaurus and a juvenile troodontid, respectively), the anatomical arrangement of the endocast more closely resembles crown birds than the arrangement found in a somatically immature specimen of the early avialan Archaeopteryx does along PC1. With age, the morphological layout of the non-avialan dinosaur endocast trends towards that of Alligator, where the mature individuals of non-avian dinosaurs and Alligator converge in their ontogenetic trajectories. This is to say that during postnatal development, the cerebrum narrows anteriorly relative to the rest of the endocast, the optic lobes become less bulbous, the hindbrain expands posterolaterally, and the degree of dorsoventral flexion decreases. P. lujiatunensis follows this trend between the perinatal and mature stages (8- and 10-year old) with the 7-year-old showing endocasts that resemble endocranial shape of subadult Alligator (Fig. 2a). The seemingly strange position of 7-year-old Psittacosaurus may be due to the dorsoventrally shallower morphology compared to the three other Psittacosaurus endocasts, which may be due to moderate degree of deformation (Supplementary Fig. 1). Juvenile hadrosaurs, such as the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and Corythosaurus (ROM 759), generally plot more closely with alligators than crown birds, but it is unclear, with current sampling, if perinatal individuals would plot more closely to crown birds as is the case with Psittacosaurus.

In general, the morphospace of cerebrum shape (Fig. 2b) generally mirrors the pattern observed in total endocranial shape, where the alligator, non-avian dinosaurs, and crown birds form clusters with partial overlap along the PC1 axis. This axis encompasses the spectrum from the more globular cerebrum in modern birds to more anteroposteriorly elongated profile in mature alligators. The orientation of the PC2 axis corresponds closely to the ontogenetic series of Alligator, which encompasses an anteroposteriorly constricted cerebrum in immature individuals to a more elongated profile in mature alligators. Overall, non-avian dinosaurs group together in the area of morphospace between mature alligators and crown birds. Among non-avian dinosaurs, the cerebrum shape of immature specimens, troodontids, and tyrannosaurids (such as the taxonomically problematic ?Nanotyrannus specimen CMNH 7541) group closest to crown birds (Fig. 2b). Endocranial shape of relatively mature ornithischian dinosaurs, including that of hadrosaurs and Psittacosaurus, overlap with that of mature alligators (Fig. 2b).

In the cerebellum shape morphospace, crown birds and Archaeopteryx form a group that is almost completely separated from alligators along PC2 (Fig. 2c). The PC1 axis is primarily associated with the anteroposterior extent and dorsoventral depth of the cerebellum. The PC2 axis mostly corresponds to the dorsoventral curvature. Non-avialan dinosaurs overlap both crown birds and alligators in cerebellar shape along both PC1 and PC2 axes. Relatively mature specimens of tyrannosaurids, troodontids, and hadrosaurs strongly overlap with relatively mature alligators. Interestingly, all the Psittacosaurus specimens lie among crown birds regardless of ontogenetic stage, although this similarity is likely due to the presence of a prominent dorsal eminence, thought to represent space occupied by non-neuronal soft tissues (e.g., venous sinus, meninges), on the cerebellum (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Fig. 1). Apart from the juvenile hadrosaurs, Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and Corythosaurus (ROM 759), all juvenile specimens of troodontids, the small-bodied tyrannosaurid specimen CMNH 7541, and other ornithischian dinosaurs, overlap with crown birds in PC2 values.

In optic lobe shape morphospace (Fig. 2d), the distinctions between alligators, non-avian dinosaurs, and crown birds are more apparent, particularly along PC1, which documents the range from the anteroposteriorly constricted and dorsoventrally elongated optic lobes in alligators to the hemispherical optic lobes in modern birds and some non-avian dinosaurs. PC2 encompasses the range from convex to topologically flat optic lobes. Alligators and crown birds overlap along PC2 due to their convex optic lobes. Optic lobes of some non-avian dinosaurs closely resemble those of alligators and crown birds. For example, the subadult Psittacosaurus (PKUP V1054) lies very close to alligators (which could be due to taphonomic deformation as noted above) and away from other congeneric specimens in PC1 values. The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451), the oviraptorid Khaan (IGM 100/973), and Archaeopteryx are adjacent to the area of morphospace occupied by crown birds.

The morphospace for brainstem shape visually separates crown birds and all other taxa sampled in this study along PC2 (Fig. 2e). The PC1 axis largely documents the ontogenetic shape changes in alligators and chickens, from a mediolaterally expanded and dorsoventrally curved brainstem in perinatal specimens to anteroposteriorly elongated and weaker dorsoventral flexion in adults. Along PC2, crown birds and the chicken ontogenetic series cluster together, while non-avian dinosaurs overlap considerably with adult and subadult alligators. More immature alligators were grouped with Archaeopteryx, relatively immature Psittacosaurus specimens (IVPP V15451, PKUP V1053, and PKUP V1054), and the immature troodontid IGM 100/1126 (Fig. 2e).

Allometric trajectories
To compare shape-to-size relationships, we visualized and tested how non-avian dinosaur endocrania differed from allometric trends in crown birds, together with developmental trajectories of Gallus and Alligator. For visualization of allometric trends, PC1 of residuals from the common allometric trend (RSC1) were plotted against scores along the allometric trend line (CAC: common allometric component) for all endocrania sampled (Fig. 3). As in previous work5, total shape variation among the endocrania of crown birds is allometrically divergent from non-avian dinosaurs and Alligator (Fig. 3a). As expected, crown birds occupy a restricted size range along the CAC axis but exhibit a high degree of shape variation along the RSC1 axis. The ontogenetic series of chickens overlaps the interspecific trajectories of the other crown birds used in this study (Fig. 3a). Whereas immature non-avian dinosaurs exhibit endocranial shapes that are distinct from both crown birds and alligators, more mature specimens of ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs converge towards the endocranial shape of mature Alligator. More immature Alligator specimens deviate further from crown birds along RSC1.

The allometric trajectory of cerebrum shape in crown birds, along with the ontogenetic series of chickens, are separate from the entire ontogenetic series of Alligator (Fig. 3b). With the exception of perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451), sampled ornithischian taxa exhibit cerebrum shapes that overlie the relatively mature alligators. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus specimen (IVPP V15451) aligns with crown birds in RSC1 values, whereas the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758), juvenile Corythosaurus (ROM 159) and more mature ornithischian dinosaurs have RSC1 values that are closer to adult Alligator. Non-avian theropods span the range of endocranial shape of alligators and modern birds, where the oviraptorid Citipati and the tyrannosaurid CMNH 7541 are within the area occupied by some of the crown birds, such as Phalacrocorax (cormorant) and Raphus (dodo). Hadrosaurs have a larger RSC1 score than the other non-avian dinosaur taxa sampled, with subadult Psittacosaurus having the lowest. Alligators span the most along RSC1, with hatchlings having large RSC1 scores that decrease notably as they mature to adulthood (Fig. 3b).

Similar to the cerebrum, allometric trajectories of the alligator and crown bird cerebella are distinct, with non-avian dinosaurs overlapping with these two taxa (Fig. 3c). Psittacosaurus, immature theropods, and non-avian maniraptoran dinosaurs group within or near crown birds, with the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and more mature non-avian dinosaurs more closely resembling adult Alligator (Fig. 3c). Adult and subadult Psittacosaurus plot with crown birds along with Tyrannosaurus (AMNH 5029) and Gorgosaurus (ROM 1247) specimens, while the juvenile and subadult hadrosaurs align more closely with Alligator (Fig. 3c). It is worth noting that non-avian dinosaur taxa positioned close to crown birds, including Zanabazar and CMNH 7541, show prominent dorsal eminence in the endocast.

For the optic lobe, crown birds and Archaeopteryx group together along the RSC1 axis (Fig. 3d). Non-avian dinosaurs loosely group together, with the oviraptorosaurs Incisivosaurus and Khaan closely resembling the optic lobe shape of crown birds and Archaeopteryx and the subadult Psittacosaurus (PKUP V1054) positioned with adult Alligator (Fig. 3d). The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and immature troodontids Zanabazar and unnamed troodontid (IGM 100/1126) are closer to the RSC1 values of crown birds than other endocasts from non-avian dinosaurs. Based on the plot, it is uncertain whether non-avian dinosaurs align more closely with the allometric trajectories of alligators and/or crown birds.

Allometric trajectories of brainstem shape of crown birds and Gallus ontogeny are mostly distinct from ontogenetic series of Alligator but converge throughout postnatal ontogeny of the brainstem (Fig. 3e). Archaeopteryx and non-avian dinosaurs of all ages align with the ontogenetic series of Alligator. In particular, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid IGM 100/1126 follow the trend line of Alligator ontogeny, away from the allometric trajectory governing scaling relationships across crown birds and chicken development. As such, the results suggest that both ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs resembled an alligator-grade scaling relationship in brainstem shape.

In addition to visual comparison of allometric trajectories, we also statistically tested the differences in allometric trajectories. The non-avian dinosaur with the most complete ontogenetic series of cranial endocasts in our study, P. lujiatunensis, was compared against allometric trends in chickens and alligators and was found to have a distinct allometric trajectory. This result is confirmed by MANOVA on full Procrustes coordinate data against log-transformed centroid size and trajectory analyses for mean angle differences (Supplementary Table 2), when compared to Gallus (MANOVA: R2=0.352; P<0.0001; trajectory analysis: mean distance=0.218, P<0.0001; angle difference=16.8°, P<0.0001) and Alligator (MANOVA: R2=0.210; P<0.0001; trajectory analysis: mean distance=0.152, P<0.0001; angle difference=11.6°, P<0.0001).
paper_content.methods:
Specimens
We amassed 85 previously published endocranial reconstructions that span 52 species of non-avian and avian dinosaurs in addition to American alligators (Supplementary Data 1). The data include interspecific sampling of 36 crown birds, a juvenile Archaeopteryx33, and 19 non-avian dinosaurs1,3,17–20,34, plus ontogenetic series of the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus; n=14), the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis; n=14), and the ornithischian Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis3,17,35 (n=4; Supplementary Fig. 1). Among non-avian dinosaurs, several isolated immature specimens of both ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs, including Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and troodontids Zanabazar and an unnamed specimen IGM 100/1126 were sampled for both ontogenetic and phylogenetic diversity19–21,36–39. The taxonomically ambiguous tyrannosaurid specimen, CMNH 7541, has been considered a relatively immature specimen within Tyrannosauridae40–45. The major results and conclusions of this study are not dependent on the taxonomic assignment of this specimen, but rather the ontogenetic stage of CMNH 7541. Considering that no specimen attributable to a tyrannosaurid similar to, and including, CMNH 7541 has preserved an external fundamental system that indicates the cessation of rapid growth and the onset of skeletal maturity32,40, we treat CMNH 7541 as an immature individual. The specimen and data acquisition protocols for Alligator and Gallus specimens were approved by Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at respective institutions (Stony Brook IACUC Protocol #236370-1; Oklahoma State University Center for Health Sciences IACUC Protocol #2015-1; American Museum of Natural History 2014). Please refer to the references listed in Supplementary Data 1 for additional details about those specimens.

Imaging and endocranial reconstructions
Endocranial reconstructions were generated from computed tomography (CT) imaging of cranial specimens. Considering the incomplete nature of the PKUP 1053 and PKUP 1054 endocasts from previous study18, they were reconstructed again for this study. We found that the original specimens and reconstructed models were of sufficient quality for morphometric analysis. These reconstructions were paired with two other Psittacosaurus specimens, IVPP V15451, and IVPP V12617, to reconstruct an ontogenetic series for the species P. lujiatunensis. The endocast of the tyrannosaurid Alioramus altai (IGM 100/1844) was retrodeformed using a local symmetrization algorithm46 implemented in the “Morpho” R package47 due to its sheared appearance. Because the combined data comprise multiple sources, the scanner, scanning parameters, and segmentation protocol naturally differ across datasets (Supplementary Data 1). Nevertheless, we considered variation in resulting shape data due to differences in these practices to be negligible compared to the large interspecific variation observed across archosaurs48. However, to adopt some standardization across endocranial reconstructions, we used the “QuickSmooth” function in Geomagic Wrap v2021 (3D Systems, Rock Hill, SC, USA) to remove cranial nerve and vascular projections from the main body of all the endocasts at the base.

Morphometric data
We adopted the same high-density 3D landmark scheme from previous studies to characterize the overall shape of endocasts and their major regions, including the cerebrum, optic lobe, cerebellum, and brainstem3,34,35 (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Table 1). The ‘patch’ tool in Landmark Editor v3.649 was used to place discrete landmarks that are anatomically defined, curve semi-landmarks that delimit regions, and surface semi-landmarks that capture the surface morphology within regions on both left and right sides of the endocast. We did not collect coordinate data from the olfactory tract and bulbs due to their incomplete preservation in the fossils, as well as their diminutive size in most crown birds. We acknowledge that endocasts are generally accurate representations of actual brain morphology among archosaurs35,50, but their correspondence is relatively low in the hindbrain due to greater presence of tissues surrounding the brain. This correspondence is lower in crocodilians27 and presumably in non-avian dinosaurs, especially the presence of dorsal eminence in some endocasts19,20,51.

The coordinate data were subjected to generalized Procrustes alignment52,53 minimizing total bending energy, allowing semi-landmarks to slide on the mesh surface54,55 using the “slider3d” and “gpagen” functions in the “Morpho”56 and “geomorph”57 R packages. After alignment, (semi-)landmarks on the right side were removed to remove redundant shape information while minimizing artifacts caused by alignment of one-sided coordinate data of bilaterally symmetric structures58,59. We extracted centroid size from the pre-aligned coordinate data, in addition to the shape data to be analyzed comprising 14 discrete landmarks, 49 curve semi-landmarks, and 56 surface semi-landmarks (Supplementary Data 2, 3). For region-specific analyses, the size and shape of each region were extracted by calculating centroid size and performing localized alignment on a subset of landmarks that characterize each region.

Time-calibrated phylogeny
To perform phylogenetic comparative analysis, we constructed a time-calibrated phylogeny that includes all the sampled species. Because the crown group sampling is equivalent to a previous study3, fossil taxa were grafted to the existing tree file (additional details on the base tree construction3). These additional taxa included Corythosaurus, Hypacrosaurus, Psittacosaurus, Gorgosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus, which were incorporated into the existing phylogeny based on the mid-point of range of first occurrence age recorded on the Paleobiology Database (paleobiodb.org). When the maximum age of a species was identical to that of its clade, the age of the internal node was set to equally bisect the parent and descendent branches (“Equal Branching Method”)60.

Analysis
All statistical analyses for this project were performed in R v4.2.161. Patterns of endocast shape variation were visualized as morphospaces for the cerebrum, cerebellum, optic lobe, and brainstem regions of the endocasts and were constructed using scores from PCA made from shape data. The functions physignal, procD.lm, and procD.pgls of the geomorph package were used to assess the level of phylogenetic signal, allometry, and evolutionary allometry, with 1000 pseudoreplications. The multivariate statistical tests outlined above were chosen due to their robusticity against type I errors and loss of power that often accompanies differences in specimen and landmark sampling62–64. Allometric trends were visualized by plotting the PC1 of residuals from the overall shape-to-size relationship against scores along this allometric relationship65. We used Morpho package’s “CAC” function to extract CAC scores and residuals from shape data. Statistical differences between endocranial shapes and allometric trajectories between clades were tested with the procD.lm function, where differences in clades were tested on data accounting for log-transformed centroid size. In addition, we used the “trajectory.analysis” function in the “RRPP” R package66 to test for differences between vectors of evolutionary and developmental shape change in total shape space.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
King et al. present a new study addressing the question of how the evolution of ontogenetic trajectories across the dinosaur-bird transition affected the origin of the modern avian brain. The authors conclude that crocodilians, non-avian dinosaurs, and modern birds show different trajectories. Although previous studies already tackled the question, the main novelty of the study relies on the inclusion of ontogenetic series of non-avian dinosaurs, which were previously neglected. Overall, I enjoyed the manuscript and I suggest publication of the study. I have a few major comments that should be addressed by the authors:
- The authors focus on heterochronic events that affected the head and the nervous system. However, what about the trend in miniaturization that is affecting the origin of birds? As stated in previous studies, multiple events of ontogenetic truncation affected the evolution of the head in the dinosaur-bird transition, but the miniaturization process leading to modern birds does not follow heterochronic trends per se. I would ask the authors to discuss this in the manuscript, considering that analyses regarding allometry per se are already present in the study.
- I agree with the general conclusions, but I don’t understand why the authors continue emphasizing that different ontogenetic trajectories among non-avian dinosaurs are surprising: the phenotype of their nervous system among non-avian dinosaurs differs from modern crocodiles and birds as a result of mosaic evolution. If we assume that an adult phenotype is the result of a specific developmental trajectory, as it is generally the case among amniotes, then this shouldn’t be surprising. I would adjust the text accordingly.
- I would ask the authors to image all ontogenetic stages of the ontogenetic series included in the study in figure 1. At the moment, only few endocasts are represented. I think this is insufficient for the scope of the study.
- I noticed that in most plots, some data points are labelled with catalogue numbers. Please, change this with the name of the taxon and ontogenetic stage: it would be very difficult for a general reader to follow the plots without having a clear expertise in this field.
- Some of the ontogenetic stages are well characterized in terms of age, but others are not. How did the authors homologize ontogenetic stages between modern and extinct species? This is fundamental to clarify considering that heterochrony requires such knowledge between compared species to infer heterochronic trends. A section in the methods is necessary. Moreover, I would add a paragraph regarding such limitations in the discussion.
- In the last part of the discussion, the authors argue that their results do not support a single heterochronic event leading to modern birds. I agree, but the original studies infer multiple heterochronic events, not just one. I would suggest the authors to revise this part of the discussion.
- Finally, there are fundamental references that are missing to justify some of the assumptions/statements in the intro and discussion that should be cited in the main text

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The manuscript "Endocranial development in non-avian dinosaurs reveals an ontogenetic brain trajectory distinct from extant archosaurs" by King and colleagues uses geometric morphometric shape analyses to compare endocranial shape of non-avian dinosaurs with that of birds and crocodylians in light of ontogenetic variation. The manuscript is well written, the methods and sampling are adequate and the results are interesting, showing an intermediate brain ontogenesis in non-avian dinosaurs, when compared with the extant phylogenetic bracket. The interpretations of the results sound fine to me. However, I some comments (listed in the PDF attached) that should be addressed. In sum, I support the publication of the manuscript in Nature Communication after a minor revision.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Dear Dr. King and colleagues,
I enjoyed reading your manuscript and found the topic really interesting. I have no doubt that this manuscript will form the starting point of a long and interesting research. Please find listed few comments that I'd like you to address.
Sincerely
Introduction
1. Line 54: “A reliable inference of evolutionary shifts in development requires sampling of adequate developmental series for non-avian dinosaurs.” Could you please explain what do you mean by “adequate”? Previous studies working on origins of the avian brain are using non-avian theropod dinosaurs that are phylogenetically close to the origins of birds (e.g., Balanoff et al. 2013, 2016; Ksepka et al. 2020; Watanabe et al. 2021). Here, you are mainly using an ontogenetic series of endocasts of the ornithischian dinosaur Psittacosaurus. Could you please consider adding few sentences in the introduction that would help to understand how this species is adequate on this topic?
2. Line 61: “Moreover, we include immature specimens of additional non-avialan dinosaurs to further define the overall developmental axis of brain morphology in non-avialan dinosaurs” Could you please add the names of the additional non-avialan dinosaurs here? Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
King et al. present a new study addressing the question of how the evolution of ontogenetic trajectories across the dinosaur-bird transition affected the origin of the modern avian brain.
The authors conclude that crocodilians, non-avian dinosaurs, and modern birds show
different trajectories. Although previous studies already tackled the question, the main
novelty of the study relies on the inclusion of ontogenetic series of non-avian dinosaurs,
which were previously neglected. Overall, I enjoyed the manuscript and I suggest publication
of the study. I have a few major comments that should be addressed by the authors:
- The authors focus on heterochronic events that affected the head and the nervous system.
However, what about the trend in miniaturization that is affecting the origin of birds? As
stated in previous studies, multiple events of ontogenetic truncation affected the evolution of
the head in the dinosaur-bird transition, but the miniaturization process leading to modern
birds does not follow heterochronic trends per se. I would ask the authors to discuss this in
the manuscript, considering that analyses regarding allometry per se are already present in
the study.
We have incorporated a section comparing the heterochronic signal we observe in brain
evolution to the trend in miniaturization occurring along the bird-line dinosaurian lineage:
“Our results suggest that paedomorphosis plays a role in the total endocranial form and
evolution of the avian brain where the form of the bird brain more resembles that of juvenile
non-avialan dinosaurs. The shift from a non-avialan dinosaur endocranial form to that of an
avian form is best explained through paedomorphosis rather than just miniaturization.
Miniaturization of the body including the brain – was a stepwise process that reduced the
body mass along stem birds and with further reductions in body sizes occurring in avialans
and pygostylian birds28,29. And while the reduction of the brain size may follow a sustained
miniaturization and has been shown to occur in faster rates among bird-line theropods than
other non-avialan dinosaur lineages30, miniaturization does not explain the expression of
juvenile non-avialan dinosaur traits along the bird brain (see also Torres et al. 2021).” [new
Ln 282-291].
- I agree with the general conclusions, but I don’t understand why the authors continue
emphasizing that different ontogenetic trajectories among non-avian dinosaurs are
surprising: the phenotype of their nervous system among non-avian dinosaurs differs from
modern crocodiles and birds as a result of mosaic evolution. If we assume that an adult
phenotype is the result of a specific developmental trajectory, as it is generally the case
among amniotes, then this shouldn’t be surprising. I would adjust the text accordingly.
We agree with the reviewer’s comment that if the adult phenotype is different, then the
allometric trajectories would be different given that the earliest stages of brain development
resemble one another across vertebrates. However, how they differ throughout ontogenetic
series could be insightful, given that several non-avian dinosaurs exhibit endocranial shapes
that closely resemble adult alligators. For example, we could anticipate that the ontogenetic
trajectories of some non-avian dinosaurs could converge to Alligator trajectories. In addition,
we argue that our results showing shared ontogenetic shape trajectories between
ornithischian and theropod taxa is surprising, given disparate neuroanatomical shape
observed and reported across non-avian dinosaurs. Nevertheless, we have modified and
clarified the statements that allude to the “surprising” factor of our results based on the
reviewer’s comment.
- I would ask the authors to image all ontogenetic stages of the ontogenetic series included
in the study in figure 1. At the moment, only few endocasts are represented. I think this is
insufficient for the scope of the study.
We have included endocast images of intermediate ontogenetic stages to Fig. 1. We
decided to not include all specimens for two reasons: (1) we believe adding the intermediate
ontogenetic stages provide information about the overall ontogenetic trends; and (2) the
figure would become very crowded as a main text figure.
- I noticed that in most plots, some data points are labelled with catalogue numbers. Please,
change this with the name of the taxon and ontogenetic stage: it would be very difficult for a
general reader to follow the plots without having a clear expertise in this field.
Our logic was to include specimen number when there are multiple specimens we sampled

juvenile tyrannosaur that has been interpreted as Tyrannosaurus rex or a separate taxon–
Nanotyrannus) or undescribed taxa (IGM 100/1126, a troodontid) as their collections

How did the authors homologize ontogenetic stages between modern and extinct species?
This is fundamental to clarify considering that heterochrony requires such knowledge

necessary. Moreover, I would add a paragraph regarding such limitations in the discussion.

And yes, references 17 and 18 refer to Psittacosaurus, but 19 through 21 indicate where the
extra ontogenetic dinosaur data came from.
Material and Methods

We have now added a column that identifies each specimen to a higher classification that is

did not find any mention of that in the text.
Yes, this Archaeopteryx specimen (WDC CSG 100) has been shown to be juvenile based on
Erickson et al. 2009.
3. Lines 323-325: “The taxonomically ambiguous tyrannosaurid specimen, CMNH 7541, is
considered a juvenile form of Tyrannosaurus rex or of a distinct taxon Nanotyrannus in this
study”. This sentence is a little bit confusing. In your results, CMNH 7541 is clearly indicated
as a juvenile specimen, so why this is not clearly stated in the Mat & Meth?
This statement has been rearranged to say “The taxonomically ambiguous tyrannosaurid
specimen, CMNH 7541, has been considered a relatively immature specimen within
Tyrannosauridae39–43. (Ln 340-342)

We have now added the following statement to clarify our meaning of the importance of

this study are not dependent on the taxonomic assignment of this specimen, but rather the
ontogenetic stage of CMNH 7541. Considering that no organism attributable to a
tyrannosaur similar to, and including, CMNH 7541 has preserved an external fundamental
system that indicates the cessation of rapid growth and the onset of skeletal maturity39,45, we
treat CMNH 7541 as an immature individual” (Ln 342-346)

package due to its sheared appearance.” This sentence, in my opinion, should be placed in

We agree. The suggested statement has been moved to the following section.
In addition, please state clearly the specimen names for which you have reconstructed the

IVPP V 15451 and IVPP V12731 were reconstructed. The reviewer is correct that the

in the Zhou et al (2017) study – the pituitary fossa and area around the anterior olfactory
apparatus, in particular – were able to be reconstructed in better detail. However,
considering that both the published and reconstructed versions of the PKUP specimens
preserved the morphology necessary to perform our statistical tests, the degree of
completeness in both versions of models is sufficient. To reflect this, we have added
“Considering the incomplete nature of the PKUP 1053 and PKUP 1054 endocasts18, they
were reconstructed again for this study. We found that the original specimens and
reconstructed models were of sufficient quality for morphometric analysis. These
reconstructions were paired with two other Psittacosaurus specimens, IVPP V15451 and
IVPP V12617, to reconstruct an ontogenetic series for the species P. lujiatunensis.” (Ln 355-
359)
6. In Figure 1c, please indicate the corresponding landmark numbers to help in the
identification of the red points.
We have added numbers for discrete landmarks corresponding to the numbering we list in
Table S1.
In the caption of Figure 1, please remove the space between lines 535 and 536. In addition,
although it is provided in other figures, please consider stating the color code in the caption
of Figure 1.
The errant space has been deleted and branch color scheme has been explained in the

7. I do not understand the definition of the 13th landmark provided in Table S1. Why “6
(reused)”? In addition, please consider adding information about the extent to which
landmarks can be placed accurately on the endocasts.
We have added an explanation for how Landmark 6 is treated in the table caption for Table
S1.
8. Line 353: “We acknowledge that endocasts are generally accurate representations of
actual brain morphology”. Yes, in birds but it depends on brain regions in other archosaurs.
Please rephrase the sentence as it sounds like a statement for all archosaurs whereas you
indicate that variability may exist within the clade in the following sentences.
Sentence updated to “We acknowledge that endocasts are generally accurate
representations of actual brain morphology among archosaurs18,33...” to indicate that we are
specifically talking about archosaurs (Ln 376-378)
Results
1. Lines 85-88: “Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid
(IGM 100/1126), as well as the juvenile tyrannosaurid (CMNH 7541), also occupy an
intermediary position between crown birds and non-avialan archosaurs along PC1 (Fig. 2a).”
What about the other immature non-avian dinosaurs? Could you please indicate their

specimens?
We have now added “All other juvenile taxa maintain similarly high PC2 scores as CMNH
7541 but have higher PC1 scores. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and
juvenile troodontid (IGM 100/1126), overlap in PC2 values as neo- and perinatal Gallus (Fig.
2a).” to explain the pattern exhibited by the remaining juvenile taxa used in this study. The

unnamed troodontid. The hadrosaurs in our sample exhibit similar differences when you
compare the juvenile Corythosaurus and Lambeosaurus specimens in Figure 2a. It is
possible that ontogenetic differences plays a part in the differences, although it is unclear at
this moment why non-avialan dinosaur taxa show varying degrees of dorsal eminence. This
section has also been moved up to the preceding paragraph (Ln 94-96).
2. Lines 91-93: “In the case of IVPP V15451 and IGM 100/112691 (Psittacosaurus and a
troodontid, respectively), the anatomical arrangement of the brain more closely resembles
crown birds than the early avialan Archaeopteryx.” I am a little bit confused, maybe I don’t

specimen share more similarities with Archaeopteryx than with crown birds. Could you
please clarify your statement?
Certainly. You are correct in that the two dinosaur endocrania share a lot in common with
Archaeopteryx; however, our statement is meant to note that both the troodontid and
perinate Psittacosaurus lie more closely to crown birds than the Archaeopteryx specimen

the endocast more closely resembles crown birds than the arrangement found in a juvenile

102)

Especially, because the features you are giving in the next sentences (lines 96-98) look like

We have calculated Procrustes shape distance between each non-avian dinosaur to adult
Alligator, then plotted and regressed distances against centroid size, showing that larger and
more mature dinosaurs gradually converge to the adult endocast shape of Alligator. We do

dinosaur endocast has lower shape distance to Alligator endocast.

Here, we are specifically referencing crown birds. This statement is now clarified to say
“…the anatomical arrangement of the endocast more closely resembles crown birds than the
arrangement found in a juvenile specimen of the early avialan Archaeopteryx does along
PC1.” (Ln 100-102)

The most likely explanation is that one of the two subadults exhibits some kind of
dorsomedial deformation that is bilaterally distributed, particularly around the midbrain.
There is difficulty in interpreting which would be the more likely culprit considering that PKUP
1053 and PKUP 1054 are the only subadult Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis endocrania
currently segmented. From personal observation, the endocast of PKUP 1053 preserves
more anatomy and was interpreted to have a better-defined dorsal eminence than PKUP

PKUP 1054, we interpret that the re-organization of the endocranium to be true considering

and statistical difference from the perinate and adult specimens. We have added the
following to help explain the difference pointed out by the reviewer: “The seemingly strange
position of 7-year-old Psittacosaurus may be due to the dorsoventrally shallower morphology

109-112)

manner similar to oviraptors and troodontids.” I disagree, the results considering the

This section has been reworded to say “The morphospace for brainstem shape visually
separates crown birds and all other taxa sampled in this study along PC2 (Fig. 2e). The PC1
axis largely documents the ontogenetic shape changes in alligator and chicken, from a

150-157)

The reviewer is correct and juvenile hadrosaurs are more similar to alligators in endocranial

group that is separated from alligators along PC2 (Fig. 2c)” Yes and no, we can see a small
overlap.
Section changed to read “In the cerebellum shape morphospace, crown birds and
Archaeopteryx form a group that is almost completely separated from alligators along PC2
(Fig. 2c)” for better accuracy (Ln 128-129)

juvenile hadrosaurs, Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and Corythosaurus (ROM 759), all juvenile

tyrannosaurids, troodontids, and hadrosaurs strongly overlap with relatively mature
alligators. Interestingly, all the Psittacosaurus specimens lie among crown birds regardless

troodontids, the tyrannosaurid CMNH 7541, and other ornithischian dinosaurs, overlap with

Correct. We have changed this segment to say “. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus

Lambeosaurus (ROM 758), juvenile Corythosaurus (ROM 159) and more mature

dinosaurs more closely resembling adult Alligator (Fig. 3c).” The end of the sentence

Correct. We also notice that this sentence seems a little repetitive with the next sentence.
The sentence commented on has been reworded as follows to incorporate the reviewer’s
comments and better incorporate it with the following sentence: “Psittacosaurus, immature
theropods, and non-avialan maniraptoran dinosaurs group within or near crown birds, with

resembling adult Alligator (Fig. 3c)” (Ln 186-189)

along with Tyrannosaurus (AMNH 5029) and Gorgosaurus (ROM 1247) specimens, while
the juvenile hadrosaur Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) aligns more closely with Alligator.” Please
indicate Tyrannosaurus (AMNH 5029) and Gorgosaurus (ROM 1247) on Fig. 3. The juvenile
Corythosaurus also aligns with alligators right?

specimens, while the juvenile and subadult hadrosaurs align more closely with Alligator (Fig.

resembling the optic lobe shape of crown birds and Archaeopteryx and the subadult
Psittacosaurus (PKUP V1054) positioned with adult Alligator (Fig. 3d)” (Ln 194-197)

Zanabazar and unnamed troodontid (IGM 100/1126) are similar in RSC1 value to crown
birds” They seems to have closer RSC1 values with crown birds but not really similar
This is a fair point. We have clarified this statement to say “The perinatal Psittacosaurus
(IVPP V15451) and immature troodontids Zanabazar and unnamed troodontid (IGM
100/1126) are close to the RSC1 values of crown birds than other endocasts from non-
avialan dinosaurs” (Ln 197-199)
Discussion
1. Lines 226-228: “Indeed, they begin somewhat avian-like among perinatal and juvenile
individuals and broadly converge to more alligator-grade endocranial morphology. Because
this allometric trajectory occurs in both coelurosaurian and ornithischian non-avian
dinosaurs,….” Both sentences are a little bit oversimplified, you are not considering the
variability you found in your results (the other ornithischian dinosaurs for example do not
show such a pattern right?).
After consideration, we disagree that this sections has been oversimplified. The reviewer is
very much correct that there is interspecific variability between the endocranial partitions.
However, this particular section is discussing the results of the total endocranial shape.
Considering that the total shape is the sum of the granular parts, and we discuss the
allometric shape implications for all of the specimens used in the study, we risk speculation if
we were to include more in this particular section. We do, however, delve deeper into the
variability the reviewer refers to in the following section.
2. Lines 235-236: “In cerebrum, cerebellum, and optic lobe shapes, non-avialan dinosaurs
resemble more those of crown birds than alligators”. You basically said in your results that
“Based on the plot, it is uncertain whether [optic-lobes in] non-avialan dinosaurs align with
the allometric trajectories of alligators and/or crown birds.” (lines 195-196). Again, this
statement seems a little bit oversimplified to me and why are not considering other
ornithischian dinosaurs?
Lines 235-236 (now 242-244) refers to the morphometric shape of the cerebrum,
cerebellum, and optic lobes whereas lines 195-196 (now 200-201) refer to the allometric
trajectories. In regards to the oversimplification, the taxonomic trends are discussed for the
total shape, cerebrum, cerebellum, optic lobes, and brainstem earlier in the manuscript in
their respective paragraphs under the ‘Endocranial shape morphospaces’ and ‘Allometric
trajectories’ subsections. The section the reviewer brings up is meant to compare all taxa
broadly and is therefore all inclusive of both ornithischian and saurischian specimens in the
term ‘‘non-avialan’ dinosaur’’
3. Lines 239-240: “these outcomes imply that non-avialan dinosaurs underwent distinct brain
development compared to crocodilians” At least in Psittacosaurus, not sure that such a rule
can be established here from the other ornithischian dinosaurs.
We posit that all dinosaur endocrania analysed in our manuscript show a growth pattern that
is distinct from crocodilians. Yes, the more mature dinosaurs come very close to overlapping
alligators in total brain shape, but the subadults and juveniles strongly diverge in form from

where non-avian dinosaurs and alligators arrive at nearly the same point in maturity but take
different routes to get there – both intraspecifically and interspecifically.
4. Line 247: “Besides the optic lobe shape being closer to crown birds” I agree closer with
birds than with alligators, but also distinct from birds
We have rephrased this sentence to say “Besides the optic lobe shape being closer to, yet
distinct from, crown birds…” (Ln 254-255)
5. Lines 248-249: “the brainstem shape of ornithischian dinosaurs visually aligns with the
allometric trajectory of alligators (Fig. 3d), whereas that of non-avialan dinosaurs, particularly
immature specimens, aligns more closely with crown birds (Fig. 3e).” I think a word is
missing here, I mean ornithischian dinosaurs are non-avialan dinosaurs, no? Also you are
saying in your results about the brainstem: “As such, the results suggest that both
ornithischian and non-avialan dinosaurs resembled an alligator-grade scaling relationship in
brainstem shape” (lines 202-204). I am a little bit confused here
You are correct and this was poor word choice on our part; we should not have separated
ornithischians from the rest of the dinosaurs. We have corrected both points the reviewer
has made to say “the brainstem shape of ornithischian dinosaurs visually aligns with the
allometric trajectory of alligators (Fig. 3d), whereas that of non-ornithischian dinosaurs,
particularly immature specimens, aligns more closely with crown birds (Fig. 3e)” (Ln 255-
257) and “As such, the results suggest that both ornithischian and saurischian dinosaurs
resembled an alligator-grade scaling relationship in brainstem shape”, respectively (Ln 207-
209).
6. Line 257, please remove the dash before “Specifically”
Removed
7. Lines 276-278: “Our results suggest that paedomorphosis plays a role in the total
endocranial form and evolution of the avian brain where the form of the bird brain more
resembles that of juvenile non-avialan dinosaurs.” Not all non-avialan dinosaurs, only
Psittacosaurus.
This is true for Psittacosaurus as well as troodontids (and to a lesser degree, Tyrannosaurus
and Lambeosaurus) when you consider the total shape of the endocranium. Troodontidae is
phylogenetically close to, but not part of, Avialae; thus, making our statement true for at least
one clade of ornithischian and saurischian dinosaur. Moreover – and, admittedly, more
tenuously – most of the non-avialan dinosaurs used in this study had endocrania
morphologies in their juvenile forms that were closer to avians than their adult forms across
PC1. While this does not hold the same weight as the evidence given by the juvenile
Psittacosaurus and troodontid, it does support that the juveniles of non-avialan dinosaurs
had endocrania that were more ‘avian-like’ than adults
Response to reviewers:
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
Dear authors,
Thank you for sending the revision of your manuscript. All my comments have been taken into

R.A

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Modern birds possess highly encephalized brains that evolved from non-avian dinosaurs. Evolutionary shifts in developmental timing, namely juvenilization of adult phenotypes, have been proposed as a driver of head evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition, including brain morphology. Testing this hypothesis requires a sufficient developmental sampling of brain morphology in non-avian dinosaurs. In this study, we harness brain endocasts of a postnatal growth series of the ornithischian dinosaur Psittacosaurus and several other immature and mature non-avian dinosaurs to investigate how evolutionary changes to brain development are implicated in the origin of the avian brain. Using three-dimensional characterization of neuroanatomical shape across archosaurian reptiles, we demonstrate that (i) the brain of non-avian dinosaurs underwent a distinct developmental trajectory compared to alligators and crown birds; (ii) ornithischian and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs shared a similar developmental trajectory, suggesting that their derived trajectory evolved in their common ancestor; and (iii) the evolutionary shift in developmental trajectories is partly consistent with paedomorphosis underlying overall brain shape evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition; however, the heterochronic signal is not uniform across time and neuroanatomical region suggesting a highly mosaic acquisition of the avian brain form.

---

## Introduction

The evolutionary origin of highly encephalized brains in modern birds is not only of interest to avian neuroscience but also has implications for how large brains evolve across vertebrates, including humans. Disentangling how the brain of crown birds (“Aves”) evolved requires study of brain anatomy ancestral to crown birds—that of non-avian dinosaurs. Using skulls and cephalic endocasts (internal molds of the braincase) as proxies for brain shape and size, previous studies have revealed that the evolutionary assembly of the avian brain form proceeded in a mosaic and homoplastic manner from the ancestral dinosaurian pattern1–11. While the tempo and mode of avian brain evolution is well established by recent studies, the mechanism underlying major neuroanatomical transformation along the dinosaur-bird transition remains uncertain3,12. Previous studies have proposed that a mixture of heterochronic processes within the cranium, particularly progenesis (truncation of the ancestral developmental period) and accelerated peramorphosis (evolutionarily driven increases in developmental rates), may underlie major changes to the brain architecture from ancestral archosaurian forms to crown birds3,11–16. However, a good developmental series of neuroanatomical morphologies for non-avian dinosaurs has been lacking to date; and crucial evidence is needed for a reliable inference of evolutionary shifts in brain development along the dinosaur-bird transition.

In this study, we examine an ontogenetic series of endocasts of the ornithischian dinosaur Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis, spanning perinatal to somatically mature individuals (<1-, 7-, 8-, and 10-year-old individuals) that were recently described17,18 (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Fig. 1). This allows for an unprecedented look into how the neuroanatomy of a non-avialan dinosaur species changes with age. We incorporate this developmental dataset into an interspecific dataset of archosaurian endocranial morphology which also includes postnatal ontogenetic series of the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus domesticus) and American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis) as an outgroup3 (Fig. 1a, b). Moreover, we include immature specimens of additional non-avialan dinosaurs17–21 (Lambeosaurus, Corythosaurus, tyrannosaurids, Zanabazar, and an unnamed troodontid; Supplementary Data 1) to further define the overall developmental axis of brain morphology in non-avialan dinosaurs (i.e., excluding Archaeopteryx considered here to be a basal avialan). Using a landmark-based geometric morphometric characterization of endocranial shape (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Table 1), the study aims to investigate how the magnitude and direction of developmental shape changes in brain morphology in non-avian dinosaurs compare to (i) the domestic chicken and the American alligator and (ii) the principal axis of brain shape evolution along the dinosaur-bird transition to evaluate whether heterochronic processes, particularly progenesis, underlie the origins of the highly derived avian brain. In our reporting, endocranial regions are referred to by their underlying soft-tissue features (i.e., “cerebrum” rather than “impression of the cerebrum”).

Here, we show that the endocranial form of non-avian dinosaurs developed and evolved uniquely when compared to crown birds and Alligator mississippiensis. We demonstrate that ornithischians and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs share a common shape-to-size relationship that guides their brain development and evolution. Regional morphometric analyses of endocranial developmental trajectories reveal that non-avian dinosaurs collectively exhibit a mosaic of avian and crocodilian modes of allometric trajectories wherein the cerebrum and optic lobe regions of immature non-avialan dinosaurs resemble those of extant birds whereas the brainstem region follows the trajectory of the crocodilians. Our results thus support a paedomorphic trend occurring along the dinosaur-bird transition that is localized to some but not all regions of the brain.

---

## Results

Endocranial shape morphospaces
To visualize total and regional endocranial shape variation, morphospaces were constructed based on principal components (PC) axes of endocast shape data (Fig. 2). In the morphospace of total endocranial shape, lower PC1 scores are associated with posterolaterally expanded cerebra, ventrally oriented optic lobes, anteroposteriorly compact hindbrains, and higher dorsoventral flexion with respect to both cephalic and pontine flexures as defined by Lautenschlager and Hübner22. Lower PC2 scores correspond to elongated cerebra, dorsoventrally extended optic lobes, anteroposteriorly shortened cerebellum, and greater dorsoventral flexion along the brainstem. As expected, total endocast shape data closely reflect the results found in previous geometric morphometric work where crown birds, alligators, and non-avian dinosaurs individually form clusters along PC1, with Archaeopteryx positioned between crown birds and non-avialan archosaurs along PC1 (Fig. 2a)3. Ornithischian and non-avialan theropod dinosaurs overlap with each other, and mature individuals of both groups strongly overlap with mature endocranial shape of Alligator along PC1 and PC2. With the exception of 7-year-old Psittacosaurus (IVPP V12731), endocasts of immature non-avialan dinosaurs generally exhibit lower PC1 scores closer to the crown bird cluster. The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid (IGM 100/1126), as well as the small-bodied, purportedly immature tyrannosaurid specimen (CMNH 7541), occupy an intermediary position between crown birds and non-avialan archosaurs along PC1 (Fig. 2a). All other juvenile taxa maintain similar PC2 scores as CMNH 7541 but have higher PC1 scores. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid (IGM 100/1126), overlap in PC2 values as neo- and perinatal Gallus (Fig. 2a).

During development, the immature non-avialan dinosaur endocasts exhibit a posterolaterally expanded cerebrum, more ventrally oriented optic lobes, anteroposteriorly compressed hindbrain, and greater degree of dorsoventral flexion. In the case of IVPP V15451 and IGM 100/1126 (perinate Psittacosaurus and a juvenile troodontid, respectively), the anatomical arrangement of the endocast more closely resembles crown birds than the arrangement found in a somatically immature specimen of the early avialan Archaeopteryx does along PC1. With age, the morphological layout of the non-avialan dinosaur endocast trends towards that of Alligator, where the mature individuals of non-avian dinosaurs and Alligator converge in their ontogenetic trajectories. This is to say that during postnatal development, the cerebrum narrows anteriorly relative to the rest of the endocast, the optic lobes become less bulbous, the hindbrain expands posterolaterally, and the degree of dorsoventral flexion decreases. P. lujiatunensis follows this trend between the perinatal and mature stages (8- and 10-year old) with the 7-year-old showing endocasts that resemble endocranial shape of subadult Alligator (Fig. 2a). The seemingly strange position of 7-year-old Psittacosaurus may be due to the dorsoventrally shallower morphology compared to the three other Psittacosaurus endocasts, which may be due to moderate degree of deformation (Supplementary Fig. 1). Juvenile hadrosaurs, such as the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and Corythosaurus (ROM 759), generally plot more closely with alligators than crown birds, but it is unclear, with current sampling, if perinatal individuals would plot more closely to crown birds as is the case with Psittacosaurus.

In general, the morphospace of cerebrum shape (Fig. 2b) generally mirrors the pattern observed in total endocranial shape, where the alligator, non-avian dinosaurs, and crown birds form clusters with partial overlap along the PC1 axis. This axis encompasses the spectrum from the more globular cerebrum in modern birds to more anteroposteriorly elongated profile in mature alligators. The orientation of the PC2 axis corresponds closely to the ontogenetic series of Alligator, which encompasses an anteroposteriorly constricted cerebrum in immature individuals to a more elongated profile in mature alligators. Overall, non-avian dinosaurs group together in the area of morphospace between mature alligators and crown birds. Among non-avian dinosaurs, the cerebrum shape of immature specimens, troodontids, and tyrannosaurids (such as the taxonomically problematic ?Nanotyrannus specimen CMNH 7541) group closest to crown birds (Fig. 2b). Endocranial shape of relatively mature ornithischian dinosaurs, including that of hadrosaurs and Psittacosaurus, overlap with that of mature alligators (Fig. 2b).

In the cerebellum shape morphospace, crown birds and Archaeopteryx form a group that is almost completely separated from alligators along PC2 (Fig. 2c). The PC1 axis is primarily associated with the anteroposterior extent and dorsoventral depth of the cerebellum. The PC2 axis mostly corresponds to the dorsoventral curvature. Non-avialan dinosaurs overlap both crown birds and alligators in cerebellar shape along both PC1 and PC2 axes. Relatively mature specimens of tyrannosaurids, troodontids, and hadrosaurs strongly overlap with relatively mature alligators. Interestingly, all the Psittacosaurus specimens lie among crown birds regardless of ontogenetic stage, although this similarity is likely due to the presence of a prominent dorsal eminence, thought to represent space occupied by non-neuronal soft tissues (e.g., venous sinus, meninges), on the cerebellum (Fig. 1a; Supplementary Fig. 1). Apart from the juvenile hadrosaurs, Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and Corythosaurus (ROM 759), all juvenile specimens of troodontids, the small-bodied tyrannosaurid specimen CMNH 7541, and other ornithischian dinosaurs, overlap with crown birds in PC2 values.

In optic lobe shape morphospace (Fig. 2d), the distinctions between alligators, non-avian dinosaurs, and crown birds are more apparent, particularly along PC1, which documents the range from the anteroposteriorly constricted and dorsoventrally elongated optic lobes in alligators to the hemispherical optic lobes in modern birds and some non-avian dinosaurs. PC2 encompasses the range from convex to topologically flat optic lobes. Alligators and crown birds overlap along PC2 due to their convex optic lobes. Optic lobes of some non-avian dinosaurs closely resemble those of alligators and crown birds. For example, the subadult Psittacosaurus (PKUP V1054) lies very close to alligators (which could be due to taphonomic deformation as noted above) and away from other congeneric specimens in PC1 values. The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451), the oviraptorid Khaan (IGM 100/973), and Archaeopteryx are adjacent to the area of morphospace occupied by crown birds.

The morphospace for brainstem shape visually separates crown birds and all other taxa sampled in this study along PC2 (Fig. 2e). The PC1 axis largely documents the ontogenetic shape changes in alligators and chickens, from a mediolaterally expanded and dorsoventrally curved brainstem in perinatal specimens to anteroposteriorly elongated and weaker dorsoventral flexion in adults. Along PC2, crown birds and the chicken ontogenetic series cluster together, while non-avian dinosaurs overlap considerably with adult and subadult alligators. More immature alligators were grouped with Archaeopteryx, relatively immature Psittacosaurus specimens (IVPP V15451, PKUP V1053, and PKUP V1054), and the immature troodontid IGM 100/1126 (Fig. 2e).

Allometric trajectories
To compare shape-to-size relationships, we visualized and tested how non-avian dinosaur endocrania differed from allometric trends in crown birds, together with developmental trajectories of Gallus and Alligator. For visualization of allometric trends, PC1 of residuals from the common allometric trend (RSC1) were plotted against scores along the allometric trend line (CAC: common allometric component) for all endocrania sampled (Fig. 3). As in previous work5, total shape variation among the endocrania of crown birds is allometrically divergent from non-avian dinosaurs and Alligator (Fig. 3a). As expected, crown birds occupy a restricted size range along the CAC axis but exhibit a high degree of shape variation along the RSC1 axis. The ontogenetic series of chickens overlaps the interspecific trajectories of the other crown birds used in this study (Fig. 3a). Whereas immature non-avian dinosaurs exhibit endocranial shapes that are distinct from both crown birds and alligators, more mature specimens of ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs converge towards the endocranial shape of mature Alligator. More immature Alligator specimens deviate further from crown birds along RSC1.

The allometric trajectory of cerebrum shape in crown birds, along with the ontogenetic series of chickens, are separate from the entire ontogenetic series of Alligator (Fig. 3b). With the exception of perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451), sampled ornithischian taxa exhibit cerebrum shapes that overlie the relatively mature alligators. Notably, the perinatal Psittacosaurus specimen (IVPP V15451) aligns with crown birds in RSC1 values, whereas the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758), juvenile Corythosaurus (ROM 159) and more mature ornithischian dinosaurs have RSC1 values that are closer to adult Alligator. Non-avian theropods span the range of endocranial shape of alligators and modern birds, where the oviraptorid Citipati and the tyrannosaurid CMNH 7541 are within the area occupied by some of the crown birds, such as Phalacrocorax (cormorant) and Raphus (dodo). Hadrosaurs have a larger RSC1 score than the other non-avian dinosaur taxa sampled, with subadult Psittacosaurus having the lowest. Alligators span the most along RSC1, with hatchlings having large RSC1 scores that decrease notably as they mature to adulthood (Fig. 3b).

Similar to the cerebrum, allometric trajectories of the alligator and crown bird cerebella are distinct, with non-avian dinosaurs overlapping with these two taxa (Fig. 3c). Psittacosaurus, immature theropods, and non-avian maniraptoran dinosaurs group within or near crown birds, with the juvenile Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and more mature non-avian dinosaurs more closely resembling adult Alligator (Fig. 3c). Adult and subadult Psittacosaurus plot with crown birds along with Tyrannosaurus (AMNH 5029) and Gorgosaurus (ROM 1247) specimens, while the juvenile and subadult hadrosaurs align more closely with Alligator (Fig. 3c). It is worth noting that non-avian dinosaur taxa positioned close to crown birds, including Zanabazar and CMNH 7541, show prominent dorsal eminence in the endocast.

For the optic lobe, crown birds and Archaeopteryx group together along the RSC1 axis (Fig. 3d). Non-avian dinosaurs loosely group together, with the oviraptorosaurs Incisivosaurus and Khaan closely resembling the optic lobe shape of crown birds and Archaeopteryx and the subadult Psittacosaurus (PKUP V1054) positioned with adult Alligator (Fig. 3d). The perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and immature troodontids Zanabazar and unnamed troodontid (IGM 100/1126) are closer to the RSC1 values of crown birds than other endocasts from non-avian dinosaurs. Based on the plot, it is uncertain whether non-avian dinosaurs align more closely with the allometric trajectories of alligators and/or crown birds.

Allometric trajectories of brainstem shape of crown birds and Gallus ontogeny are mostly distinct from ontogenetic series of Alligator but converge throughout postnatal ontogeny of the brainstem (Fig. 3e). Archaeopteryx and non-avian dinosaurs of all ages align with the ontogenetic series of Alligator. In particular, the perinatal Psittacosaurus (IVPP V15451) and juvenile troodontid IGM 100/1126 follow the trend line of Alligator ontogeny, away from the allometric trajectory governing scaling relationships across crown birds and chicken development. As such, the results suggest that both ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs resembled an alligator-grade scaling relationship in brainstem shape.

In addition to visual comparison of allometric trajectories, we also statistically tested the differences in allometric trajectories. The non-avian dinosaur with the most complete ontogenetic series of cranial endocasts in our study, P. lujiatunensis, was compared against allometric trends in chickens and alligators and was found to have a distinct allometric trajectory. This result is confirmed by MANOVA on full Procrustes coordinate data against log-transformed centroid size and trajectory analyses for mean angle differences (Supplementary Table 2), when compared to Gallus (MANOVA: R2=0.352; P<0.0001; trajectory analysis: mean distance=0.218, P<0.0001; angle difference=16.8°, P<0.0001) and Alligator (MANOVA: R2=0.210; P<0.0001; trajectory analysis: mean distance=0.152, P<0.0001; angle difference=11.6°, P<0.0001).

---

## Methods

Specimens
We amassed 85 previously published endocranial reconstructions that span 52 species of non-avian and avian dinosaurs in addition to American alligators (Supplementary Data 1). The data include interspecific sampling of 36 crown birds, a juvenile Archaeopteryx33, and 19 non-avian dinosaurs1,3,17–20,34, plus ontogenetic series of the domestic chicken (Gallus gallus; n=14), the American alligator (Alligator mississippiensis; n=14), and the ornithischian Psittacosaurus lujiatunensis3,17,35 (n=4; Supplementary Fig. 1). Among non-avian dinosaurs, several isolated immature specimens of both ornithischian and non-avian theropod dinosaurs, including Lambeosaurus (ROM 758) and troodontids Zanabazar and an unnamed specimen IGM 100/1126 were sampled for both ontogenetic and phylogenetic diversity19–21,36–39. The taxonomically ambiguous tyrannosaurid specimen, CMNH 7541, has been considered a relatively immature specimen within Tyrannosauridae40–45. The major results and conclusions of this study are not dependent on the taxonomic assignment of this specimen, but rather the ontogenetic stage of CMNH 7541. Considering that no specimen attributable to a tyrannosaurid similar to, and including, CMNH 7541 has preserved an external fundamental system that indicates the cessation of rapid growth and the onset of skeletal maturity32,40, we treat CMNH 7541 as an immature individual. The specimen and data acquisition protocols for Alligator and Gallus specimens were approved by Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at respective institutions (Stony Brook IACUC Protocol #236370-1; Oklahoma State University Center for Health Sciences IACUC Protocol #2015-1; American Museum of Natural History 2014). Please refer to the references listed in Supplementary Data 1 for additional details about those specimens.

Imaging and endocranial reconstructions
Endocranial reconstructions were generated from computed tomography (CT) imaging of cranial specimens. Considering the incomplete nature of the PKUP 1053 and PKUP 1054 endocasts from previous study18, they were reconstructed again for this study. We found that the original specimens and reconstructed models were of sufficient quality for morphometric analysis. These reconstructions were paired with two other Psittacosaurus specimens, IVPP V15451, and IVPP V12617, to reconstruct an ontogenetic series for the species P. lujiatunensis. The endocast of the tyrannosaurid Alioramus altai (IGM 100/1844) was retrodeformed using a local symmetrization algorithm46 implemented in the “Morpho” R package47 due to its sheared appearance. Because the combined data comprise multiple sources, the scanner, scanning parameters, and segmentation protocol naturally differ across datasets (Supplementary Data 1). Nevertheless, we considered variation in resulting shape data due to differences in these practices to be negligible compared to the large interspecific variation observed across archosaurs48. However, to adopt some standardization across endocranial reconstructions, we used the “QuickSmooth” function in Geomagic Wrap v2021 (3D Systems, Rock Hill, SC, USA) to remove cranial nerve and vascular projections from the main body of all the endocasts at the base.

Morphometric data
We adopted the same high-density 3D landmark scheme from previous studies to characterize the overall shape of endocasts and their major regions, including the cerebrum, optic lobe, cerebellum, and brainstem3,34,35 (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Table 1). The ‘patch’ tool in Landmark Editor v3.649 was used to place discrete landmarks that are anatomically defined, curve semi-landmarks that delimit regions, and surface semi-landmarks that capture the surface morphology within regions on both left and right sides of the endocast. We did not collect coordinate data from the olfactory tract and bulbs due to their incomplete preservation in the fossils, as well as their diminutive size in most crown birds. We acknowledge that endocasts are generally accurate representations of actual brain morphology among archosaurs35,50, but their correspondence is relatively low in the hindbrain due to greater presence of tissues surrounding the brain. This correspondence is lower in crocodilians27 and presumably in non-avian dinosaurs, especially the presence of dorsal eminence in some endocasts19,20,51.

The coordinate data were subjected to generalized Procrustes alignment52,53 minimizing total bending energy, allowing semi-landmarks to slide on the mesh surface54,55 using the “slider3d” and “gpagen” functions in the “Morpho”56 and “geomorph”57 R packages. After alignment, (semi-)landmarks on the right side were removed to remove redundant shape information while minimizing artifacts caused by alignment of one-sided coordinate data of bilaterally symmetric structures58,59. We extracted centroid size from the pre-aligned coordinate data, in addition to the shape data to be analyzed comprising 14 discrete landmarks, 49 curve semi-landmarks, and 56 surface semi-landmarks (Supplementary Data 2, 3). For region-specific analyses, the size and shape of each region were extracted by calculating centroid size and performing localized alignment on a subset of landmarks that characterize each region.

Time-calibrated phylogeny
To perform phylogenetic comparative analysis, we constructed a time-calibrated phylogeny that includes all the sampled species. Because the crown group sampling is equivalent to a previous study3, fossil taxa were grafted to the existing tree file (additional details on the base tree construction3). These additional taxa included Corythosaurus, Hypacrosaurus, Psittacosaurus, Gorgosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus, which were incorporated into the existing phylogeny based on the mid-point of range of first occurrence age recorded on the Paleobiology Database (paleobiodb.org). When the maximum age of a species was identical to that of its clade, the age of the internal node was set to equally bisect the parent and descendent branches (“Equal Branching Method”)60.

Analysis
All statistical analyses for this project were performed in R v4.2.161. Patterns of endocast shape variation were visualized as morphospaces for the cerebrum, cerebellum, optic lobe, and brainstem regions of the endocasts and were constructed using scores from PCA made from shape data. The functions physignal, procD.lm, and procD.pgls of the geomorph package were used to assess the level of phylogenetic signal, allometry, and evolutionary allometry, with 1000 pseudoreplications. The multivariate statistical tests outlined above were chosen due to their robusticity against type I errors and loss of power that often accompanies differences in specimen and landmark sampling62–64. Allometric trends were visualized by plotting the PC1 of residuals from the overall shape-to-size relationship against scores along this allometric relationship65. We used Morpho package’s “CAC” function to extract CAC scores and residuals from shape data. Statistical differences between endocranial shapes and allometric trajectories between clades were tested with the procD.lm function, where differences in clades were tested on data accounting for log-transformed centroid size. In addition, we used the “trajectory.analysis” function in the “RRPP” R package66 to test for differences between vectors of evolutionary and developmental shape change in total shape space.
